variants.title: Method of mixtures: specific heat of aluminium
variants.note: Aluminium stores much heat per kilogram, so 100 g warms 150 g of water by about 9 °C.

source.title: CRC Handbook of Chemistry and Physics, Heat capacity of the elements at 25 °C: Al 0.897 J/(g K); density 2.70 g/cm3

variants.title: Method of mixtures: specific heat of copper
variants.note: Copper has less than half the specific heat of aluminium, so twice the mass is used for a clear rise.

source.title: CRC Handbook of Chemistry and Physics, Heat capacity of the elements at 25 °C: Cu 0.385 J/(g K); density 8.96 g/cm3

variants.title: Method of mixtures: specific heat of brass
variants.note: Brass is the commonest solid in school calorimetry sets; its value lies between copper and zinc.

source.title: Engineering ToolBox, Metals - specific heats: brass 0.380 kJ/(kg K); density 8.5 g/cm3

variants.title: Method of mixtures: specific heat of iron
variants.note: An iron bob or cylinder: dull grey, heavier than aluminium for its size.

source.title: CRC Handbook of Chemistry and Physics, Heat capacity of the elements at 25 °C: Fe 0.449 J/(g K); density 7.87 g/cm3

variants.title: Method of mixtures: specific heat of lead (less water)
variants.method: Method of mixtures, copper calorimeter, 100 g of water
variants.note: Lead has a very small specific heat. A heavy piece and only 100 g of water keep the temperature rise (about 5 °C) large enough to read well.

source.title: CRC Handbook of Chemistry and Physics, Heat capacity of the elements at 25 °C: Pb 0.129 J/(g K); density 11.34 g/cm3

variants.title: Method of mixtures: specific heat of zinc
variants.note: Zinc is lighter than copper for its size, with almost the same specific heat.

source.title: CRC Handbook of Chemistry and Physics, Heat capacity of the elements at 25 °C: Zn 0.388 J/(g K); density 7.14 g/cm3

variants.title: Method of mixtures: specific heat of tin (less water)
variants.method: Method of mixtures, copper calorimeter, 100 g of water
variants.note: Tin's specific heat is low, so 100 g of water is used to give a rise of about 7 °C.

source.title: CRC Handbook of Chemistry and Physics, Heat capacity of the elements at 25 °C: Sn 0.228 J/(g K); density 7.27 g/cm3

variants.title: Method of mixtures: specific heat of stainless steel
variants.unknown: the specific heat of stainless steel
variants.note: An alloy: its specific heat is a little higher than that of pure iron.

source.title: Engineering ToolBox, Metals - specific heats: stainless steel 304, 0.50 kJ/(kg K); density 8.0 g/cm3
